title: Mabel and the Lost Rabbit
markdown:
Once upon a time, nestled on a hillside like a plump mushroom, stood a crooked little cottage. Inside lived a young witch named Mabel. Her eyes sparkled like freshly polished moonstones. Her heart was as warm as a sunbeam on a daisy. Her greatest joy was finding glow-moss, its soft green glow just perfect for bubbling potions. She heard rustling leaves, smelled sweet flowers, and hummed happy witchy songs.

Every day she set off into the Misty Crags, woven basket swinging, hunting shimmer-wings and the sweetest-smelling moonpetals, always humming, always imagining new brews. The Crags liked to hide things in mist and then pretend they had not. Mabel did not mind. Looking was half the fun, and humming was the other half, and glow-moss was a prize that glowed even when you stopped looking.

Until one day, chasing a firefly that glittered like a tiny captured star, she tumbled with a soft oof into moss that smelled of sunshine and earth. When she sat up, shaking pine needles from her pointy hat, she saw him: a very flustered, very fluffy white rabbit, hopping in tiny worried circles. His nose twitched like a busy clock pendulum. He looked completely lost. He whimpered, burying his nose in Mabel’s cloak, missing his own cozy bed.

“Oh, my goodness.” Soft as a moth’s wing. “You seem to have misplaced your home, little one.”

Glow-moss could wait. She scooped him up. Sweet clover, warm damp earth. “Don’t you worry your twitchy nose. We’ll find your burrow before the first stars twinkle hello.” The sky was already blushing with sunset. She decided she simply must.

Because of that, they wound through whispering pines, tall and noble, needles sighing secrets into the breeze. Mabel called the rabbit Alaric, because a lost rabbit deserves a proper name and not only a whimper. He wiggled in her arms, whiskers busy with new smells. He tried to nibble her sleeve, then a fallen pinecone that looked like a tiny brown castle, then a corner of the basket, which had opinions about teeth.

“Steady on, Alaric.” She giggled, shifting her hold. “We have a very important quest.” A cloud of worry drifted across her cheerful thoughts as the sun slipped. Burrows, she knew, were harder to find after apricot hour.

As the sky painted itself apricot and lavender they came to a cozy cave. Out came a wizard: Professor Eldrin Fizzlewick, beard like a silver waterfall, spectacles always sliding down his nose, clutching not one, not two, but what looked like a hundred maps, unfurling and flapping around his feet like startled birds.

“Ah, greetings, travellers!” Friendly distant thunder. “Lost, are we? It happens to the best of us. Which direction were you aiming for? I have a map for every single direction, and quite a few in-between!” He peered at Mabel and Alaric, then at the maps, which seemed to be dancing. One showed a river like a giant spaghetti noodle. Another was upside down and featured a laughing cloud.

Mabel had to figure out which map, or perhaps which lantern, would lead them home. Alaric discovered that the edges of one particularly ancient map tasted interesting, and began to nibble with great enthusiasm, tiny holes appearing.

“Oh dear.” She eased the paper from determined jaws. “Professor, I’m not quite sure which one is the right one. Alaric’s home is near the big twisty oak by the singing stream.”

Professor Fizzlewick peered, blinked, squinted at the setting sun. “The twisty oak? This map certainly shows a twisty oak. Or perhaps a particularly wiggly worm. And this one: a stream, or a very fast-flowing path of blueberries?” Beard quivering with indecision. Maps pointing every way at once.

Alaric’s nose kept twitching, sniffing twilight. On a nearby ledge sat a small smooth stone lantern, pulsing with a gentle warm light, much like glow-moss.

Until finally Mabel took Alaric’s little paw. “Sniff, Alaric. Sniff for home. What does your tummy tell you?”

He forgot the maps. A deep investigative sniff. He hopped down and nudged toward a faint familiar scent on the evening breeze. Mabel remembered her grandmother, another wise witch: some things are best found not by staring at maps, but by feeling them with your heart and your nose. She picked up the stone lantern.

“Professor,” clear as a little bell, “sometimes the best light is the one that shines from close by.”

She held it high. Warm on her cheeks. Pine, damp earth. A soft humming, like the forest sighing, contented. The lantern did not shout left or right. It made the next bit of ground look like a place you could trust. Alaric hopped ahead, a tiny white beacon in the beam. Professor Fizzlewick bundled his maps, somewhat haphazardly, and came too, spectacles still sliding, one map still tasting faintly of rabbit.

And so they found the big twisty oak. Alaric scampered into his burrow, safe, a tiny grateful nose-nudge, then gone. The Professor chuckled. “Remarkable. A fluffy rabbit and a little lantern.” He did not add a speech. He pushed his spectacles up, and they slid down again at once.

Ever since then Mabel looked where she was going, mostly. She still tumbled, now and then, because moss is moss. She and Alaric became dear friends, sharing glow-moss cookies near the singing stream. Sometimes, when the moon was particularly bright, they saw Professor Fizzlewick’s lantern twinkling on its ledge, a little reminder, not a lesson, just a light left on.
characters: Mabel (young witch), Alaric (rabbit), Eldrin Fizzlewick (wizard with maps)
